LightMem (arXiv 2510.18866) is the paper. It is inspired by the Atkinson–Shiffrin model of human memory and organizes memory into three stages—sensory memory, short-term memory (STM), and long-term memory (LTM)—mirroring human sleep/storage stages [2510.18866#s1.p1][2510.18866#s6.p1]. Its Light1 sensory compression keeps only tokens above a retention threshold [2510.18866#s7.p3][2510.18866#s7.p4], Light2 buffers topic segments in STM until a token threshold before summarizing [2510.18866#s8.p1][2510.18866#s8.p3], and Light3 performs sleep-time offline LTM updates [2510.18866#s9.p1]. This cuts cost dramatically: 28.25k tokens and 18.43 calls versus 1,605.81k tokens and 986.55 calls for A-MEM on LongMemEval-S [2510.18866#s10.p7], with up to 38× token and 30× API-call reductions [2510.18866#s13.p2].

They differ in whether conflicting/stale information is actively removed. HippoRAG (and HippoRAG 2) is an indexing-and-retrieval framework: it builds an LLM-extracted knowledge graph (OpenIE triples plus synonym and passage nodes) and retrieves via Personalized PageRank, with no mechanism described for detecting or resolving contradictions between old and new memories — new passages are simply added to the graph/index [2405.14831#s5.p2][2502.14802#s7.p4]. GC-Mem, by contrast, is explicitly an inference-time consistency protocol for mutable memory: it detects contradictions with a pairwise NLI conflict oracle within the retrieved candidate set and applies a temporal-dominance operator that excises older, shadowed contradictory chunks, so only the terminal state survives [2609.16073#s1.p1][2609.16073#s9.p2][2609.16073#s9.p4]. GC-Mem thus targets the Semantic Shadowing / Majority Vote Trap problem where stale and updated states are semantically equivalent and retrieval favors the majority of stale chunks [2609.16073#s2.p2][2609.16073#s6.p4], whereas HippoRAG's graph retrieval has no such pruning step. GC-Mem's effectiveness is bounded by conflict-detector recall (>50% required) [2609.16073#s20.p1].

HippoRAG (and HippoRAG 2) has no explicit mechanism for handling new or conflicting information: it is an offline indexing + retrieval framework that builds an LLM-extracted knowledge graph and retrieves with Personalized PageRank [2405.14831#s5.p2][2502.14802#s7.p4]. New passages are simply indexed into the graph, and conflicts are left to the reader/context — on FactConsolidation, HippoRAG-v2 reaches only 54.0 single-hop and 5.0 multi-hop accuracy, i.e. it largely fails to overwrite outdated facts [2507.05257#s21.p3]. GC-Mem instead handles conflicts at retrieval time: it keeps the store append-only but excises contradicted older chunks from the retrieved context via temporal dominance [2609.16073#s9.p4], reaching 97.3% Conflict Resolution Accuracy on deepseek-v3 Large versus 56.8% for Standard RAG [2609.16073#s14.p3]. So HippoRAG relies on graph indexing without conflict resolution, while GC-Mem actively filters stale/contradicted chunks out of the retrieved context.

They operate at different levels. HippoRAG (and HippoRAG 2) is an indexing/retrieval architecture, not a conflict-resolution protocol: it builds an LLM-extracted OpenIE knowledge graph with synonym edges and passage nodes, and retrieves via Personalized PageRank [2405.14831#s5.p2][2405.14831#s6.p4][2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2]. New information is handled by adding passages/triples to the graph (non-parametric continual learning) [2502.14802#s1.p1], and it has no mechanism for detecting or excising contradictory older states — the corpus pages report no update/conflict adjudication for HippoRAG. GC-Mem, by contrast, is an inference-time consistency protocol: it runs a pairwise NLI conflict oracle within the retrieved candidate set and applies temporal dominance Φ_T, excising any older chunk contradicted by a newer one, so that if a valid chunk is retrieved P(y=S_new)→1 [2609.16073#s9.p2][2609.16073#s9.p4][2609.16073#s9.p5]. It targets Semantic Shadowing, where stale and updated states coexist and dense retrieval returns the majority of stale chunks [2609.16073#s2.p2], and its efficacy is bounded by detector recall (>50% required) [2609.16073#s16.p1][2609.16073#s20.p1]. In short: HippoRAG accumulates new knowledge into a graph index without explicit conflict resolution, whereas GC-Mem explicitly detects contradictions and prunes temporally dominated (older) memories at query time [2609.16073#s1.p1].

HippoRAG (and HippoRAG 2) is a retrieval framework, not a conflict-resolution protocol: it builds an LLM-extracted knowledge graph (OpenIE triples plus synonym edges and passage nodes) and retrieves with Personalized PageRank [2405.14831#s5.p2][2405.14831#s6.p4][2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2]. It has no explicit mechanism for detecting or excising contradictory older memories; new information is simply indexed into the graph, and on contradiction-heavy benchmarks it performs poorly — HippoRAG-v2 reaches only 54.0 single-hop and 5.0 multi-hop on FactConsolidation [2507.05257#s21.p3], and 54.0/5.0 versus ReFind's 62.7/8.8 under MemoryAgentBench [2608.12888#s23.p3][2608.12888#s24.p2].

GC-Mem instead targets conflicting information directly at inference time: it keeps the store append-only but applies a temporal dominance operator Φ_T, which uses a pairwise NLI contradiction oracle κ within the retrieved candidate set to excise any older chunk contradicted by a newer one, so chained mutations collapse to the terminal state [2609.16073#s9.p2][2609.16073#s9.p4][2609.16073#s9.p5][2609.16073#s5.p2]. The two differ fundamentally: WikiLoop explicitly trains its knowledge base using downstream feedback, while HippoRAG 2's knowledge graph is built offline with no downstream signal.

WikiLoop — feedback-coupled construction. WikiLoop couples construction of an agent-native Wiki to the downstream agent that consumes it within a single role-conditioned policy [2607.26604#s1.p1]. It identifies that construction usually 'receives no signal from downstream use' as the problem it fixes [2607.26604#s1.p1]. The Builder's reward is the marginal change in navigation utility: each rollout applies one patch to an isolated copy and runs a frozen Navigator on both states, giving ΔU_affected and ΔU_guard [2607.26604#s7.p8][2607.26604#s7.p12]. The reward is ΔU_affected − λ_g[−ΔU_guard]_+ − λ_e C_edit − P_structure [2607.26604#s7.p14]. Guard queries (same-author, no page/source overlap) penalize regressions one-sidedly [2607.26604#s7.p7][2607.26604#s7.p17]. This yields affected ΔAC 12.1 and held-out ΔU 0.084 while cutting Guard Regression from 0.046 to 0.016 [2607.26604#s12.p12].

HippoRAG 2 — no downstream feedback into the KB. HippoRAG 2 builds its graph offline: an LLM extracts schemaless OpenIE triples, synonym edges are added by embedding similarity, and passages become passage nodes linked by 'contains' edges [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2]. Online, an LLM filter keeps only relevant triples as seeds before PPR [2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. The LLM is used at query time for filtering, but the page describes no mechanism by which downstream answer quality updates the graph structure — the knowledge base is fixed after indexing.

In short, WikiLoop treats downstream navigation utility as the training signal for KB edits (with guard queries against collateral damage), whereas HippoRAG 2's structured index is constructed once and only filtered at retrieval time.

They differ in whether downstream feedback is used at all. HippoRAG 2 builds its knowledge graph (OpenIE triples, synonym edges, passage nodes) offline and retrieves with query-to-triple matching, LLM triple filtering, and Personalized PageRank; its construction is not trained or corrected by downstream answer feedback — the LLM is used online only for filtering [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s9.p1][2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. WikiLoop instead couples construction and navigation in one role-conditioned policy and trains the Builder from downstream navigation utility: each candidate patch is applied to an isolated Wiki copy, a frozen Navigator is run before and after, and the reward is the guarded marginal utility difference (affected-query gain minus guard-query regression, edit cost, and structural penalty), optimized with GRPO/GSPO [2607.26604#s7.p8][2607.26604#s7.p14][2607.26604#s8.p11]. So HippoRAG 2's structured index is fixed by an offline extraction pipeline, whereas WikiLoop's structured Wiki is learned against the downstream consumer's measured performance [2607.26604#s1.p1].

respuesta: They differ in whether downstream feedback is used at all. HippoRAG 2 builds its knowledge graph (OpenIE triples plus passage nodes) with an LLM and retrieves via query-to-triple matching, LLM triple filtering, and Personalized PageRank; its construction is not trained against downstream answer quality — the LLM extractor/filter and retriever are used as-is, and improvements come from architectural choices (passage integration, recognition-memory filtering) rather than feedback-driven learning [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. WikiLoop instead explicitly couples construction to the downstream consumer: a single role-conditioned policy both builds and navigates an agent-native Wiki, and the Builder is trained on downstream navigation utility — each candidate patch is scored by the before/after utility difference under a frozen Navigator, with guard queries penalizing regressions, and optimized with GRPO/GSPO [2607.26604#s1.p1][2607.26604#s7.p8][2607.26604#s7.p14][2607.26604#s8.p11]. So HippoRAG 2's KB is a fixed, statically constructed index, whereas WikiLoop's KB is learned from downstream feedback [2607.26604#s1.p1].

pasos.argumento: HippoRAG 2 downstream feedback knowledge base construction

respuesta: WikiLoop explicitly trains its structured knowledge base (an agent-native Wiki of linked pages) using downstream feedback: a single role-conditioned policy learns both to build and to navigate the Wiki, with the Builder rewarded by the marginal change in navigation utility measured by a frozen Navigator on affected queries, minus a guard penalty for regressions on unrelated queries [2607.26604#s1.p1][2607.26604#s7.p2][2607.26604#s7.p14]. HippoRAG 2, by contrast, builds its structured knowledge base (an OpenIE triple graph with phrase, synonym, and passage nodes) offline with an LLM extractor and does not optimize construction from downstream task feedback; its online LLM use is a recognition-memory filter over retrieved triples before Personalized PageRank, and retrieval is evaluated with fixed hyperparameters rather than learned from downstream rewards [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2][2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. In short, WikiLoop closes a feedback loop from the consuming agent back into KB construction, whereas HippoRAG 2 keeps indexing and retrieval as separately specified, non-learned components [2607.26604#s1.p1][2502.14802#s1.p1].
